newsitem.title: USA: U.S. lumber industry tries to plug quota.
newsitem.headline: U.S. lumber industry tries to plug quota.

text.p: The U.S. lumber industry is trying to close what it sees as a loophole in a lumber pact that allows Canadian lumber producers to escape quotas on exports to the United States.

The U.S. lumber industry contends that Canadian lumber producers are modifying pieces called studs to exempt them from being counted as part of Canada's quota-regulated lumber exports to the United States, sources said.

Under an agreement with the United States, Canada can ship 14.7 billion board feet of lumber annually to the United States duty-free. Quantities beyond that amount are subject to a tariff of $50 per 1,000 board feet. If the excess exceeds 650 million board feet, the tariff goes to $100.

"It's not a big deal right now," said Scott Shotwell, executive director of the Coalition for Fair Lumber Imports. "It could become a big loophole because there is about four billion board feet (of normal studs) coming in a year."
"It is being done wholly to bypass the agreement," said John Ragosta, a Coalition lawyer, referring to drilled studs that have holes to accommodate electrical wires.
Studs are 2x4s (two by fours) about eight feet in length, used in walls of homes.
The Coalition, which represents about 65 percent of U.S. softwood lumber manufacturers, is trying to persuade the U.S. Customs Service to disallow the practice.
"We are talking with Customs and saying a stud is a stud," Shotwell said.
Customs officials were unavailable for comment.
Canfor Corp., a Vancouver, British Columbia-based forestry company, began producing modified studs for the Canadian market in 1996 and is now shipping them to the United States.
"It doesn't qualify under the quota, but we do pay a duty," said Ralph Eastman, Canfor's manager of corporate communications.
U.S. lumber sources said the U.S. assesses duties on imports of quota-exempt lumber, but that the duties are much lower than the tariffs would be if the quota were exceeded.
"We introduced it (the modified lumber) in Canada first and now we are trying to market it in the United States," Eastman said.
He said the modified studs account for about 3 percent to 4 percent of the firm's total production, and "what is exported to the U.S. is even smaller."
The studs are designed for the housing market and the holes were added to accommodate electrical wiring, he said.
Dave Evans, associate editor of the lumber trade publication Random Lengths, said the mill had apparently found a loophole in the Canadian-U.S. lumber agreement.
"If a significant volume of studs were drilled, that would give them (mills) room to ship other (lumber) dimensions. That would basically negate the effectiveness of the agreement," Evans said.
